Training produces a small logit gap δ \delta : two models fit to the same next-token objective approach the text’s conditional distribution as their loss falls. Over a training run, cross-family agreement rises as the loss falls and is near zero until it beats a bigram baseline ( Figures 11 and E.3 ). Experimental evidence. We take the 16 models of Section 4.1 and form 26 tokenizer-sharing pairs: 15 pythia pairs, 10 qwen2.5 pairs and one SmolLM2 pair, evaluated on 100 documents. The logit gap δ \delta of a pair is the norm of the difference of the two models’ centred next-token logits, averaged over positions and documents. Agreement ( Section 3.1 ) is computed on each tokenizer group’s character axis and applied both to the per-token marginal influence , in the row-gradient approximation of Section 4.1 , and to the unweighted ( ω ≡ 1 \omega\equiv 1 ) per-token marginal attention . Within a tokenizer group, as the logit gap grows, per-token marginal influence agreement falls, which is consistent with Theorem 1 . Validating our empirical argument, per-token marginal attention agreement falls as well. Takeaway. Sufficiently smooth models with similar next-token logits for a given input have their per-token marginal influences guaranteed to be close, under mild assumptions on the dependence patterns in the Jacobian ( Theorem 1 ). To obtain an eviction policy, we pair it with Expected Attention as the score ( Section 5.2 ). 5.1 Head budget from the per-head marginal attention Head Mass (HM) is the per-head marginal attention of Definition 3 with three choices taken from KVzip, a state-of-the-art eviction method that is expensive at run time, since it pays a second target forward per document. First, Head Mass is read on the reconstruction queries , the positions t t of a second pass in which the model repeats the context, since eviction must keep what later queries attend to. We evaluate Equation 1 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, phi-4 and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Abdin et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Each method pairs a budget with a score. AdaKV + EA ( Feng et al., 2025 ) splits the budget inside each layer per document and scores with Expected Attention (EA) ( Devoto et al., 2025 ) , a training-free scorer. KVzip ( Kim et al., 2025 ) takes both the budget and the score from a second target forward per document. AdaKV + KVzap ( Jegou & Jeblick, 2026 ) keeps the AdaKV budget and scores with a KVzip surrogate trained per target. LU-KV + EA ( Tang et al., 2026 ) takes its budget from an offline per-head table calibrated per target and scorer, and scores with EA. HM + EA takes our Head Mass budget and scores with EA. HM + Guide keeps the Head Mass budget and tilts EA, head by head, by a linear map fitted once per target ( Section F.4 ). The map predicts the KVzip+ score from the marginal attention of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, a model about fifteen times smaller than the smallest target. It probes whether a smaller model’s attention carries the eviction signal and is not meant as a practical method. We report RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) (13 tasks, 6500 documents) at context 4096 and compression 4 × 4\times , 8 × 8\times and 16 × 16\times , the factor by which the cache shrinks. Scores at context 8192 ( 8 × 8\times and 16 × 16\times ) and on LongBench ( Bai et al., 2024 ) are in Tables 14 and 15 , per-task scores in Section F.5 , and costs in Table 11 . Result analysis. Budget. Table 1 shows that the HM budget accounts for most of the gap from standard EA to KVzip. In fact, with the same scorer, HM + EA considerably improves on its baseline on every target and setting, closing most of the gap to KVzip without the double-forward on the target. HM + EA is also ahead of AdaKV + KVzap in all but one cell, and its budget is built offline in minutes and read at inference as a fixed table, with no representation access, where a KVzap surrogate trains for hours ( Table 11 ) and needs light online computation. Even though it has extra scorer calibration, LU-KV + EA is level with HM + EA on phi-4 and Llama-3.1-8B, close on Mistral-7B, and far behind on both Qwen3 targets. Averaging over pretraining text loses little: the HM budget agrees closely, head for head, with the keep rates KVzip+ realises on held-out documents ( Section F.2 ). The query set is crucial: set by the reading queries (i.e., all positions), a proportional budget ( Equation 4 ) consistently loses to the baseline AdaKV + EA with no fixed budget ( Table 13 ), showing a profile can be stable across documents and still be the wrong quantity for eviction. The cut matters less ( Section F.3 ). Score. Tilting EA by the guide’s map raises HM + EA in all but two columns, so a smaller model’s attention can carry part of the eviction signal. Takeaway. Which heads matter for eviction is a property of the model: a per-head marginal attention profile computed once recovers most of the gain of per-document signals, and a score tilted by a smaller model can further improve it. 6 Conclusions We studied attention in language models through its marginals and found that one structure per document carries two different signals. Reduced over heads, the per-token marginal attention is a property of the text: models that differ in lab, data, size, tokenizer and architecture agree on which input tokens are attended. Reduced over tokens, the per-head marginal attention is a property of the model: it is stable across documents and private to each model. We showed that the per-token profile is shared because it tracks a Jacobian statistic that similar predictors must share: smooth models with close next-token distributions have close input-output Jacobians, with marginal attention approximating its the blockwise norms. The only data assumption is that its discrete conditional distributions admit a smooth approximation good enough for independently trained models to agree on the next token. To our knowledge this is the first formal result of the kind discussed by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis ( Huh et al., 2024 ) , but it does not imply semantic convergence ( Nelson et al., 2026 ) : the shared profile separates documents without aligning strongly with classical syntactic structure.
